   tracheal stenosis, her trache was decannulated but her stoma was not
   healing.  She was admitted for surgical closure of her trache.  After
   the operation she developed subQ emphasema around her face closing her
   L eye, in her upper chest and down her arms.  She was admitted to the
   MICU to watch her airway.  She c/o pain around her throat and has
   difficulty swallowing.

   11:45AM with anesthesia, ENT, surgery at bedside.  Switched to 40% high

   Extubated successfully and on humidified O2. Pt did receive 20mg IV
   lasix at 8AM for CXR results

   Tolerating extubation at this time.
   Plan:
   Follow resp status closely. Encourage cough and deep breath. Pt to
   remain NPO for now. This is reinforced by our team with pt and her
   husband.
   Tracheal reconstruction (Tracheobronchial)
   Assessment:
   Pt has operative trach site noted from closure of old wound. Draining
   small amts yellow thick drainage.
   Action:
   After being seen by surgeon this afternoon they want it left open to
   air

   Plan:
   Follow wound drainage and for signs symptoms of further infection.

   Team asked to give lasix this AM instead of the lisinopril ordered at

   Response:
   Good response to 20mg IV lasix given this AM
   Plan:
   Follow vital signs closely and give dose of lisinopril at 8PM if pt
   able to swallow pills.

 localize the fluid collection to be drained. Images were obtained using a
 localizing grid.

 coaxial needle into the fluid collection from a left lateral approach. Local
 anesthesia with 1% was applied prior to inserting the needle.

 CT guided catheter insertion: Initially, a 12 french pigtail catheter was
 placed along the same trajectory as the initially placed coaxial needle. CT
 fluoroscopy was used to locate the position of the catheter, the tip of which
 was just anterior to the lower abdominal aorta. At this time, the patient's
 vital signs were noted to be stable with blood pressure in the 130's. This
 catheter was then withdrawn. Limited scans using CT fluoroscopy of the area
 were then performed. There was no evidence of fluid around the lower abdominal
 aorta it was determined that the aorta was not punctured, as the patient's
 vital signs remained stable for the remainder of the procedure, and a fat
 plane remained between the aorta and the collection. Following this, an 8
 french pigtail catheter, was inserted and angulated more anteriorly into the
 collection. The position of the catheter was confirmed using CT fluoroscopy.

 A small aspirate of fluid was taken, which returned sanguineous slightly
 purulent material. The material was shown to the surgical house staff who were
 present during the procedure and it was decided to continue with catheter
 placement. The pigtail was formed within the collection, and again its
 position was confirmed using CT fluoroscopy. After the catheter was placed,
 500 cc of sanguinous material was aspirated from the collection. Much of the
 cavity of the collection collapsed after this aspiration. The catheter was
 then placed to gravity drainage and an additional 200 cc of sanguinous
 material was drained.

 after placement of the pigtail catheter. Again seen is a fluid collection

developed, quite overweight gentleman.  Head, Eyes, Ears,
Nose & Throat were normal.  The neck was notable for poor
extension.  Chest was clear with distant breath sounds.  The
abdomen was obese, with a midline scar with at least two
areas of herniation.  There were no masses.  The extremities
were without cyanosis, clubbing or edema.  He was
neurologically intact.

colon carcinoma, for sigmoid colectomy following a prior
resection.  On the date of admission, he underwent a sigmoid

adhesions, but was otherwise uncomplicated.  Postoperatively,
the patient initially did quite well.  He was closely
monitored with the CIWA Scale on the floor.  Hematocrit was

had a few episodes of agitation.  However, on [**2201-2-26**], he

had increasing doses of Lopressor as well as Clonidine and
Ativan in addition to some anxiolytics.  He appeared to be
diaphoretic and tachycardic.  He also was showing signs of
some volume depletion.

Unit where he had respiratory distress and was given
intravenous resuscitation.  He required intubation and a
Foley catheter was placed with some trauma.  Creatinine level
noted to be somewhat elevated.  The working diagnosis at this
time was that the patient had alcohol withdrawal originally,
but then decompensated.  He was begun on vasopressors due to
decompensation of his hemodynamics.  After some
resuscitation, the patient underwent a CT scan which showed
no evidence of extravasation of contrast.  Changes seen in
the abdomen were consistent with his postoperative state.

was presumed secondary to high doses of vasopressors,
however, he continued to have significant mottling of his
legs.  He underwent an exploration of the right lower
extremity and right femoral embolectomy and fasciotomy to the
lower leg due to a poor blood flow.  This was done on
[**2201-2-28**].  He then developed increasing oliguria with a
rising BUN and creatinine associated with a very elevated CPK
of 28,000, which improved after his fasciotomies.  He then
seemed to stabilize to some degree with his acute renal
failure as well as question of septic picture.  He was
continued on antibiotics.

A Quinton catheter was placed and the patient was dialyzed
after some period of a bit more stability.  The patient
developed increasing amounts of instability and was unable to
be dialyzed.  He was thought perhaps to have Clostridium
difficile and was continued on Flagyl as well as other
antibiotics.  He then became more unstable and a CT scan was
performed, which showed a pelvic abscess consistent with an
anastomotic leak.  This was drained radiologically when the
patient was quite unstable and had an elevated coagulation
profile.  This was despite aggressive attempts at repleting
coagulation parameters.

This drainage was attempted because the patient was in florid
sepsis and it seemed to be the only alternative to the
potential of saving his life.  After the intervention,
originally some bloody pus type fluid was removed, however,
then he began to have increasing amounts of bleeding from the
area.  He became even more hemodynamically unstable.  Because
of persistent septic picture and the inability to keep his
blood pressure up despite maximum resuscitation, the patient
was made comfort measures and allowed to expire.

The presumptive scenario was that the patient developed some
alcohol withdrawal and decompensation leading to a low-flow
state, which required vasopressors.  This caused the
difficulties with his legs and elevated CPKs and thrombosis
as well as a low flow state to the bowel which then
progressed to a delayed anastomotic dehiscence with sepsis.

1.  Carcinoma of the colon.
2.  Sepsis.
3.  Delayed anastomotic dehiscence secondary to low flow.
4.  Diabetes mellitus.
5.  Hypertension.

immediately postoperatively, anticipating returning to the
Operating Room in three days for a planned posterior spinal
fusion with instrumentation procedure.  She received
perioperative antibiotics.  She was placed in TEDs stockings
and sequential compression devices for DVT prophylaxis.  The

decompressive laminectomies at that time secondary to severe

intraoperatively secondary to disseminated intravascular
coagulopathy. She lost 7 liters of blood intraoperatively and was
transfused with 14 units of packed red cells, 18 units of
fresh frozen plasma, multiple units of cryoprecipitate, and
multiple platelet transfusions.  The chest tube was removed
intraoperatively.

Intensive Care Unit in a guarded condition.  Upon extubation
two days postoperatively from the second procedure, she was
subsequently transferred to the Orthopedic floor in a stable
condition.  A TLSO brace was fabricated for her.  Following
her transfer to the floor, she slowly progressed with respect
to institution of a diet and return of bowel and bladder
function.  She was transitioned from IV to oral narcotic
analgesics.

The patient was seen by Physical Therapy and was ambulating
with assistance up in her TLSO brace.  The patient did
receive multiple additional transfusions following her second
procedure, ultimately achieving a stable hematocrit of 34.
She was felt to be an excellent candidate for a
rehabilitation stay where she could continue her
postoperative rehabilitation and recovery.

Neurologically, the patient had normal strength and sensation
throughout the lower extremities postoperatively.  Her
incisions remained clean, dry, and intact, and without any
evidence of infection during her hospital course.

most likely, with possible drugs including levofloxacin, Lasix,

argatroban due to concerns about HIT, but was then switched to
lepirudin due to concerns about elevated LFT's.  He was placed
